title: 3 PhD positions opening at QMUL in early 2027
text: I will be recruiting three PhD students in early 2027. I am particularly looking for candidates working on Internet measurement, standardisation, governance and/or its economics. For examples of my work in these areas, see my research interests and the IRTF RASP Research Group. I am also open to discussing interesting ideas outside this scope. If you would like to explore potential opportunities, get in touch.

title: Interested in doing a PhD with me? FAQ
text:
I am always interested in hearing from prospective PhD students whose research interests connect with mine. If you are considering applying to work with me, here are a few things to know.

Before getting in touch, have a look at my research interests and recent publications. You do not need to propose something I am already working on, but it should relate to my interests and/or expertise. If so, email me with a brief introduction, your CV, why you would like to do a PhD with me, and the research area or questions you want to explore. This can range from a few initial ideas to a more developed research proposal (see below). If the topic looks promising, I will be happy to discuss it further and give some feedback as you develop the proposal. Any formal application must ultimately go through the usual Queen Mary application process.

Application

You can find information about the formal application process in the QMUL EECS PhD application guidance. As part of applying to work with me, I would also like you to prepare a research proposal (see below).

Funding can come from different sources. EECS advertises funded PhD studentships, and Queen Mary maintains a broader guide to PhD funding. I may also have funding linked to particular projects. You can find information about my funded projects and any open positions, and you are welcome to ask me about possible funding.

Research proposal

If you want to work with me, I would like you to prepare a short research proposal. For me, this is one of the best ways to judge whether there is the basis for a PhD. I am interested not only in the topic, but also in how you identify a problem, develop research questions, and think about ways of addressing them.

Around 4–6 pages is a reasonable length. The proposal should be clear and concise: if you need more than 10 pages, it is probably worth spending more time working out exactly what the core research problem and main ideas are. It should focus on the research rather than on you as a person. If your previous experience is directly relevant to the proposed work, it makes sense to mention it.

A good proposal will normally:

  • Introduce and motivate the area. What is the broader problem, and why is it interesting or important?
  • Discuss relevant existing work. What do we already know? What has been tried? Where are the gaps or limitations? This should establish the context rather than become an exhaustive literature review. A good starting point is recent work in the main conferences and journals in the area.
  • Define the problem. Be as precise as you can about what is missing and the research question you want to address. Why does it matter, and why is it non-trivial?
  • Describe the research you would do. How would you tackle the problem? What methods, data, systems, experiments or other forms of evaluation might you use? You are not expected to know the answer already: finding that out is part of the PhD.
  • Be balanced. Motivation and related work should set up the research rather than dominate the proposal. A common mistake is to spend most of the proposal explaining why an area is important and then say little about the problem you actually want to study. A useful check is whether your proposal addresses the questions in the Heilmeier Catechism.

Discussion and feedback

Discussion is an important part of the process. I am happy to brainstorm research ideas with you and discuss different ways to approach a problem. These conversations help me understand how you tackle problems, develop ideas, and respond when those ideas are questioned or alternatives are suggested. They also help us work out whether doing a PhD together would work well.

I am also happy to comment on a draft proposal. However, the proposal should be your work and reflect your own ideas; it is not something we will write together.

I can only offer a limited number of rounds of feedback and discussion. Try to make the most of them: come to meetings with specific questions or ideas to explore, and send drafts once there is enough substance for useful feedback.

Writing

The aim of the proposal is not to demonstrate your writing prowess. I care much more about clear ideas and reasoning, and I understand that English may not be your first language. I recommend following Orwell's rules for writing: avoid clichés and unnecessary jargon, prefer fewer and shorter words and active over passive voice, and disregard any of these rules when necessary.

You may use tools to help with writing, but the research questions, reasoning and ideas must be yours. I will not reply to or provide feedback on content that is purely AI-generated.

For further guidance, I recommend the advice for prospective PhD students from Cambridge Computer Science (Timothy Jones), Cambridge Computer Science (Robert Mullins), St Andrews Computer Science and the University of Edinburgh. These are worth reading when preparing your proposal, and they have also informed some of the guidance on this page.
